title: What is ATO Fraud and How Can You Protect Payees from Payout Interception?
summary: Is a hijacked payee account sending your payouts to the wrong place? See how ATO fraud works and how a payouts API can stop it before money moves.
body_markdown:
**Account takeover attacks are rising, and payouts are one of the quickest ways for criminals to cash in. This guide explains how the scheme works and what a smarter payout setup can do about it.**


A contractor logs in on a Friday evening, updates their bank details, and requests a withdrawal. By Monday, the money is gone and the real payee is writing to your support team to ask where their earnings went. Nobody on your side did anything unusual. The payout system simply did what it was told.


That is the quiet danger of account takeover. The attacker does not need to break into your systems. They only need one payee's login and a payout process that trusts whichever bank details arrive last. For a lean finance team, the outcome is a refund you did not budget for, a frustrated user, and a week of cleanup.


The scale of the problem explains why this deserves attention.[Javelin's 2026 Identity Fraud Study](https://allaboutcookies.org/account-takeover-costliest-fraud-type) found that 6 million Americans had an account taken over in 2025, an 18% increase from 2024, with losses above $15 billion. The FBI reported more than 5,100 complaints and over $262 million in losses from ATO schemes in the[first eleven months of 2025](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251125) . Overall, consumers told the[FTC they lost $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025](https://www.ftc.gov/node/330116) , a record high.


## What is ATO Fraud?


Account takeover (ATO) fraud happens when a criminal gains control of a legitimate account, usually with stolen or phished login details, and uses it to move money or steal information. The FBI warns that attackers often pose as bank support staff to talk account owners into sharing passwords and one-time codes, as outlined in its[public service announcement on ATO schemes](https://www.ic3.gov/PSA/2025/PSA251125) .


In a payout setting, the target is the payee account. Once inside, the attacker swaps the bank account or wallet, requests a withdrawal, and the funds are gone before the real owner notices. A[reliable payouts API](https://usedots.com/platform/payouts-api/) matters here because it decides whether a routing change is trusted automatically or questioned first.


## Why Payout Interception is So Hard to Catch


Most payout systems work in a straight line. Details are updated, the withdrawal is requested, and the transfer is sent. Each step looks routine on its own, and the attacker is counting on that.


The damage also lands on the platform. Payees blame the business that holds the funds, and Javelin found that ATO victims spent an average of[17 hours resolving the fraud](https://allaboutcookies.org/account-takeover-costliest-fraud-type) .


## How Can You Prevent Account Takeover Fraud in Payments?


The most effective step is to add a checkpoint between a risky change and the money leaving. A[flexible payouts API](https://usedots.com/platform/payouts/) lets you build that checkpoint into the payout flow itself, rather than relying on someone to spot a problem in a spreadsheet. Good account takeover fraud prevention at the payout layer usually includes these steps:


- **Watch withdrawal behavior.** Flag sudden shifts, such as a first withdrawal after months of inactivity or a payout request that arrives minutes after a login from a new device.
- **Hold funds when routing details change.** If a payee updates a bank account or routing number from an unfamiliar IP address, keep the balance in escrow until the change is verified.
- **Confirm through a second channel.** Out-of-band authentication, such as a prompt sent to a verified phone or email, proves the real payee made the change.
- **Verify identity up front.** Identity checks at onboarding make it harder for a stolen account to pass as a trusted one later.
- **Keep a clear record.** Logged changes and holds make disputes easier to resolve and reviews easier to pass.


Speed still matters. Payees expect to be paid quickly, so the goal is to challenge only the transfers that look risky and let everything else move without delay.
